scenes.title: Why do big brands disappear in AI answers?
scenes.sub: Brands everyone knows, missing from AI recommendations
items: Starbucks: coffee shop questions in Seattle
scenes.say: Nespresso, Armani, Starbucks. Brands everyone knows. But when you ask AI about coffee machines, perfume or coffee shops, are these brands recommended? We measured it, and the answer is often no. ChatGPT did not recommend Nespresso in any of sixteen coffee machine answers. Armani was missing from all thirty-two live-search fragrance answers. And Starbucks showed up in only six of forty-eight answers in its own hometown, Seattle. In this video, we look at five patterns in the data, and their likely causes.

scenes.title: How we measured it

boxes.d: 8 questions per category; no brand names in the questions.
ChatGPT and Claude searched the web; Gemini answered from memory.
The same categories were asked in Turkish and in English.
How many answers recommended each brand, counted per AI.

scenes.say: Here's the method. With AI SaaSavran, we asked eight real buyer questions in categories like coffee machines, fragrance, TVs, robot vacuums, gaming laptops, phones, sneakers and private hospitals. No brand names appear in the questions. ChatGPT and Claude answered with live web search. We asked Gemini the same questions without search, so it answered from memory only. Then we counted how many answers recommended each brand, separately for each AI.

scenes.title: Well-known, but not recommended
scenes.note: Live search: ChatGPT + Claude. Gemini sample is small (16 answers).
scenes.say: Let's start with the table. Nespresso was recommended in only three of thirty-one live-search answers, but Gemini, answering from memory, recommended it in thirteen of sixteen. Tom Ford shows the same pattern: three with live search, ten on Gemini. In Turkey, Adidas was recommended in nine of thirty-two live-search answers, and in fifteen of sixteen on Gemini. Armani and Philips TVs were never recommended with live search. These brands are not unknown. The Gemini sample is small, so read these gaps as a signal, not a hard rule. Let's look at the likely causes.

scenes.title: Likely cause 1: fame lives in memory, not in today's reviews
scenes.note: Our interpretation: memory reflects past fame; live search reflects today's review sites.
scenes.say: Pattern one: AI answering from memory and AI searching the web don't recommend the same brands. Our interpretation: fame lives in memory, not in today's reviews. An AI answering from memory, like Gemini, remembers brands people have talked about for years. That may explain why it recommended Nespresso in thirteen of sixteen answers. But when ChatGPT and Claude search the web, they read what today's review sites say. If Nespresso isn't at the top of current best coffee machine lists, you'd expect AI not to recommend it. A brand's past fame does not automatically turn into recommendations in live-search AI.

scenes.title: Likely cause 2: you're not the category specialist
scenes.note: Observation: for "best X" questions, the brand known as the specialist was picked.
scenes.say: Pattern two: big brands that make everything get zero in some categories. The likely cause: they aren't seen as the category specialist. Philips is a huge brand, but when we asked about robot vacuums, it was recommended in zero of twenty-four answers, while Roborock was recommended in twenty-two. For coffee machines, Siemens got zero and De'Longhi nineteen. For gaming laptops, Dell got three and Lenovo nineteen. Our data shows AI answering a best robot vacuum question with brands known as specialists, while giant brands that make everything stay invisible.

scenes.title: Pattern 3: one AI recommends you, another never does
scenes.note: Likely explanation: ChatGPT cites fewer sources and builds shorter lists.
scenes.say: Pattern three: one AI recommends you, another never does. Claude recommended Xiaomi phones in thirteen of twenty-four answers; ChatGPT in none of thirty-two. For MSI gaming laptops, Claude eight, ChatGPT zero. In Turkey, Claude recommended Liv Hospital seven times; ChatGPT never did. In our measurements, ChatGPT cited fewer sources per answer. We can't prove that's the cause, but a likely explanation is that a brand that misses its short list disappears on that AI. That's why measuring your brand on only one AI can be misleading.

scenes.title: Pattern 4: change the question, the brand drops
scenes.say: Pattern four: change the question, and the brand drops. Oura is one of the most recommended smart rings in the US. But when we asked for the ring with the longest battery life, it was recommended in zero of six answers. For a smart ring without a subscription, also zero, because Oura charges a monthly fee. Starbucks wasn't mentioned at all for coffee near Pike Place Market. A brand can be well known overall, and still lose to another brand on the specific question a customer asks, about price, battery, subscription or location.

scenes.title: Pattern 5: local brands are weak even at home
scenes.sub: Questions in Turkish, live search from Turkey · recommendations
scenes.note: Our interpretation: local brands need a presence on the review sites AI actually reads.
scenes.say: Pattern five: local brands can be weak even in their home market. In Turkey, for coffee machine questions asked in Turkish, Philips was recommended in twenty-three of twenty-nine answers. Local brands Arzum got five, and Fakir zero. For TVs, Samsung got seventeen, while Turkish brand Vestel was recommended only once. Even in Turkish, AI mostly reads big English-language review sites. A likely cause: a local brand that isn't covered there can stay outside AI recommendations, even at home.

scenes.title: Starbucks, in its own city
scenes.sub: 8 coffee shop questions in Seattle · 48 live-search answers
scenes.note: All 6 answers citing Yelp mentioned Storyville.
scenes.say: We can see all of these reasons in one example: Starbucks, in its own city, Seattle. It appeared in only six of forty-eight live-search answers, and all six came from the question about where a tourist should go. For the best espresso, local roasters, or coffee near Pike Place Market, Starbucks was never mentioned. Gemini, answering from memory, mentioned it in ten of fourteen answers. The fame is there, but other cafes stand out in today's local guides and on Yelp, and live-search AI puts them first.

scenes.title: Big brand or not: four steps

boxes.d: Not overall awareness: whether you're recommended for each real question.
You can be zero on ChatGPT and strong on Claude.
Who was recommended instead of you, based on what?
Be on your category's review sites with correct, current facts.

scenes.say: So what should you do? We suggest four steps. First, look past overall awareness and measure question by question: know whether you're recommended for each question your customers ask. Second, measure each AI separately; you can be zero on ChatGPT and strong on Claude. Third, find out why you lost: who was recommended instead of you, and based on what? Fourth, be present on your category's current review sites with correct information. Live-search AI reads what's written today.
